mcqs.question: Which of the following electron‑dot structures correctly shows the bonding in ethane (C₂H₆) compared with methane (CH₄)?

options.A: CH₃—CH₃ with each carbon surrounded by three H atoms and a single C–C bond.
options.B: CH₄ with carbon surrounded by four H atoms and no C–C bond.
options.C: C≡C with each carbon having two bonds.
options.D: CH₂=CH₂ with each carbon having two H atoms and a double bond.

mcqs.answer: CH₃—CH₃ with each carbon surrounded by three H atoms and a single C–C bond.
mcqs.explanation: In ethane each carbon forms four covalent bonds: three with hydrogen and one with the other carbon, giving the structure shown in option A. Methane’s structure (option B) lacks a C–C bond, so option A correctly compares the two molecules.

mcqs.learning_point: Relate bonding to diversity of carbon compounds
mcqs.question: Why does carbon give rise to a far greater variety of compounds than most other elements?

options.A: Carbon can form only single bonds, limiting the number of possible structures.
options.B: Carbon can form up to four covalent bonds and can bond to itself, creating long chains and rings.
options.C: Carbon only forms ionic bonds with metals, which restricts its chemistry.
options.D: Carbon’s valence shell can hold only two electrons, so it forms very few bonds.

mcqs.answer: Carbon can form up to four covalent bonds and can bond to itself, creating long chains and rings.
mcqs.explanation: Carbon’s tetravalency allows it to make four covalent bonds, and its ability to bond with other carbon atoms (catenation) enables the formation of chains, branched structures, and rings, leading to an enormous number of possible compounds. The other statements are incorrect descriptions of carbon’s bonding behavior.

mcqs.question: What does the tetravalency of carbon mean?

options.A: Carbon can share two electrons with other atoms.
options.B: Carbon can lose four electrons to become C⁴⁺.
options.C: Carbon can form four covalent bonds by sharing four pairs of electrons.
options.D: Carbon can form only one bond at a time.

mcqs.answer: Carbon can form four covalent bonds by sharing four pairs of electrons.
mcqs.explanation: Tetravalency refers to carbon’s ability to use its four valence electrons to form four covalent bonds, each involving a shared pair of electrons. Options A, B, and D misstate the concept.

mcqs.question: Catenation in carbon chemistry refers to:

options.A: Formation of double bonds between carbon atoms.
options.B: Bonding of carbon exclusively with oxygen atoms.
options.C: Carbon’s ability to attract electrons strongly.
options.D: Carbon’s ability to bond with another carbon atom, forming chains or rings.

mcqs.answer: Carbon’s ability to bond with another carbon atom, forming chains or rings.
mcqs.explanation: Catenation is the property of carbon to link with other carbon atoms, producing long chains, branched structures, and cyclic compounds. Options A, B, and C describe different phenomena.

mcqs.question: Which statement correctly defines covalent bonding and distinguishes it from ionic bonding?

options.A: Covalent bonding involves the sharing of electron pairs between atoms, unlike ionic bonding where electrons are transferred.
options.B: Covalent bonding occurs only in metals, while ionic bonding occurs only in non‑metals.
options.C: Covalent bonds are always weaker than ionic bonds.
options.D: Covalent bonding does not involve electrons at all.

mcqs.answer: Covalent bonding involves the sharing of electron pairs between atoms, unlike ionic bonding where electrons are transferred.
mcqs.explanation: In covalent bonds atoms share electrons to achieve stable configurations; ionic bonds result from complete transfer of electrons, producing oppositely charged ions. Options B, C, and D are inaccurate.

mcqs.question: Which description correctly represents the electron‑dot structure of carbon dioxide (CO₂)?

options.A: Carbon single bonded to two oxygen atoms, each oxygen bearing three lone pairs.
options.B: Carbon double bonded to two oxygen atoms, each oxygen bearing two lone pairs.
options.C: Carbon triple bonded to one oxygen and single bonded to another oxygen, with appropriate lone pairs.
options.D: Carbon bonded to one oxygen with a double bond and to another oxygen with a single bond.

mcqs.answer: Carbon double bonded to two oxygen atoms, each oxygen bearing two lone pairs.
mcqs.explanation: In CO₂, carbon forms two double bonds with oxygen atoms. Each oxygen atom has two lone pairs, satisfying the octet rule. Option B correctly describes this; the other options misrepresent bond order or lone‑pair count.

mcqs.learning_point: Relate bonding to diversity of carbon compounds
mcqs.question: Which of the following compounds best illustrates how catenation contributes to the diversity of carbon compounds?
mcqs.explanation: Hexane contains a chain of six carbon atoms, showing catenation. The ability of carbon atoms to link in various lengths and branching patterns leads to many different hydrocarbons. Methane has no C–C bond, CO₂ lacks C–C bonds, and water contains no carbon.

mcqs.question: In a molecule, a carbon atom is shown forming three single bonds with three hydrogen atoms. Which statement is true about this carbon atom?

options.A: The carbon atom already satisfies tetravalency.
options.B: The carbon atom will form a double bond with one of the hydrogens.
options.C: The carbon atom will lose an electron to become positively charged.
options.D: The carbon atom needs to share one more electron pair to complete its tetravalency.

mcqs.answer: The carbon atom needs to share one more electron pair to complete its tetravalency.
mcqs.explanation: Carbon requires four covalent bonds (four shared electron pairs). With only three bonds to hydrogen, it still needs one more shared pair, either by bonding to another atom or forming a multiple bond. Options A, B, and C are incorrect interpretations.
